analysis.one_liner: Raises the gun-buying age to 21 for certain semiautomatic rifles, and cracks down on trafficking, ghost guns, bump stocks, and large magazines.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 223-204 on June 8, 2022, but the Senate never voted on it, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This package of gun-safety rules would bar licensed dealers from selling certain semiautomatic rifles and shotguns that accept large magazines to anyone under 21, with exceptions for active-duty military and police. It creates new federal crimes for straw purchases and gun trafficking, requires serial numbers on so-called ghost guns, regulates bump stocks like machine guns, and bans the future manufacture and sale of magazines holding more than 15 rounds. It also makes it a federal offense to store a gun where a child or a prohibited person can get it, and funds programs to distribute gun locks and safes.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and families in homes where guns are present, and communities affected by mass shootings and street-level gun trafficking. Young people under 21 would no longer be sold high-capacity semiautomatic rifles at licensed dealers; police would get new trafficking and straw-purchase charges carrying up to 10 years in prison; untraceable homemade guns would have to be serialized; and households would face penalties if a child or a legally prohibited resident can reach an unsecured firearm.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children, families, and communities hit by gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Bars licensed dealers from selling semiautomatic centerfire rifles or shotguns that can accept magazines holding more than 5 rounds to anyone under 21, with exceptions for active-duty military and authorized government employees who carry guns.
Creates new federal crimes for straw purchases and gun trafficking, punishable by up to 10 years in prison, with trafficked firearms subject to forfeiture.

Requires all firearms to be traceable by banning ghost guns without serial numbers, treating unfinished frames and receivers as regulated firearms, and restricting machines built solely to make firearms to licensed manufacturers.

Makes it a federal offense to store a gun where a minor or a legally prohibited resident is likely to access it, with a $500 fine per violation and up to 5 years in prison if a child or prohibited person gets the gun and someone is injured or killed; dealers must include a locking device with every handgun, rifle, and shotgun sale, and a new grant program would spend $10 million a year helping states and tribes distribute safe-storage devices.

Regulates bump stocks under federal firearms laws as machine-gun-like devices and bans the future import, sale, manufacture, transfer, and possession of magazines holding more than 15 rounds, while letting people keep ones they already own and funding voluntary buy-backs.

analysis.who_pays: Gun manufacturers and licensed dealers bear the compliance burden and lose some sales: no more high-capacity semiautomatic rifle sales to 18-to-20-year-olds, no new large magazines to make or sell, serialization and record-keeping requirements, and a required storage device and notice with each firearm sold. Adults aged 18 to 20 lose the ability to buy certain semiautomatic rifles and shotguns. Taxpayers fund the new grant programs.

drawbacks.text: The under-21 rule covers only semiautomatic centerfire rifles and shotguns capable of accepting magazines over 5 rounds; an 18-to-20-year-old could still legally buy many other long guns, so the age restriction leaves significant gaps.

The magazine ban applies only to future manufacture and sales; magazines over 15 rounds already owned when the bill passes can be kept indefinitely, and the buy-back program is voluntary, so millions of large-capacity magazines would remain in circulation.

Critics of such laws argue that barring sales to 18-to-20-year-old adults denies them a constitutional right to purchase common rifles, an argument courts have taken seriously in litigation over similar state age limits. Supporters also concede the $500 base fine for unsafe storage is modest, rising only when a child or prohibited person actually gets the gun and someone is hurt or killed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The restrictions target the specific features most associated with mass-shooting fatalities (high-capacity semiautomatic rifles sold to very young buyers) and with street-level violence (trafficking, straw purchases, untraceable guns), while the grandfathered magazine stock and the narrow scope of the age rule limit how much the law could actually change. The cost falls mainly on dealers and manufacturers in the form of compliance and lost sales, and on young adults' purchasing options, not on the general public. The design is incremental rather than comprehensive, but the trade-off leans toward public safety.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill on June 6, 2022, after a 25-19 markup vote, and the Ways and Means Committee was discharged so the bill could reach the floor.
The House passed the bill 223-204 on June 8, 2022, with 218 of 220 Democrats voting yes and only 5 of 208 Republicans joining them.

Before final passage, the House held separate votes on each of the bill's seven titles, all of which passed; the narrowest margins were on Title IV (safe storage, 220-205) and Title VI (large magazines, 220-207), and the one Republican motion to recommit the bill to committee failed 198-228.
The Senate received the bill on June 9, 2022, and no further action was ever taken on it; it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in the Senate without a vote, gun manufacturers and licensed dealers avoided the new sales restrictions, serialization requirements, and storage-device mandates, and no new federal gun controls took effect from this bill. Communities affected by gun violence received nothing from this bill, though Congress passed a narrower, bipartisan gun package separately that summer.

for.name: Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and reported it out of the Judiciary Committee on a 25-19 vote.

for.name: 177 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and delivered 218 of the 223 votes for final passage.

against.name: 203 of 208 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, after voting no on retaining each major title of the bill.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Received the bill from the House on June 9, 2022, and never scheduled it for a Senate vote; with the filibuster in place, the bill had no realistic path without 60 votes and the chamber instead pursued a narrower bipartisan deal.

sides.party_line_note: On final passage, 218 of 220 House Democrats voted yes while only 5 of 208 Republicans did; one Republican-proposed motion to send the bill back to committee failed on party lines as well, 198-228.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from selling certain semiautomatic rifles and shotguns to buyers under 21, ban new manufacture and sale of magazines over 15 rounds, require serial numbers on frames and receivers, include a locking device and safe-storage notice with every firearm sold, and expose them to new trafficking-related liability. Dealers would face compliance costs and lost sales; the industry lobbied against the package.

industries.industry: Ghost gun parts and home gunmaking equipment sellers
industries.note: The bill would ban unserialized 'ghost guns,' define unfinished frames and receivers as regulated firearms requiring serial numbers, and make it unlawful to sell machines whose sole or primary function is manufacturing firearms to anyone but a licensed manufacturer, closing off the unserialized DIY gun market.

Every handgun, rifle, and shotgun sale would have to include a secure storage or safety device, and a new $10-million-a-year federal grant program would buy and distribute storage devices to the public through states, tribes, and local governments.
